extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, ethnologists, and educated readers interested in the conditions and history of animal domestication
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the biological and behavioural conditions that make a wild species likely (or unlikely) to become permanently domesticated by humans, using historical and ethnological evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardiness
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be able to shift for itself and to thrive, although it is neglected; since, if it wanted much care, it would never be worth its keep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator: rapidity with which the species establishes itself in new lands (e.g., goats and hogs thriving on islands, horses on the Pampas, sheep and ox in Australia, dogs in Oriental towns). Anti-pattern: species requiring continual close care are poor candidates. Scoring notes: assess survivability under neglect, ability to forage independently, and success when introduced to new environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fondness of Man
rubrics_metrics.description: It must cling to man, notwithstanding occasional hard usage and frequent neglect; if the animal had no natural attachment to our species, it would fret itself to death, or escape and revert to wildness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and counterexamples: reindeer can be too independent and difficult to manage (milkable only by lassoing), North American reindeer not domesticated for this reason; moose are relatively easy to tame; zebras are unmanageable and prone to 'mulish' wild outbursts. Assess natural attachment to humans, tolerance of mistreatment, tendency to remain with human groups rather than revert to the wild.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire of Comfort (temperamental suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comfort-loving temperament that prefers domestic routine over the excitement of wild life is necessary; animals that thoroughly enjoy the strong stimuli of wild life cannot be domesticated, only tamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: guinea-fowl have little care for comfort and barely fall within domestication (only in inclement seasons); elephants, large and powerful, not dependent on man for protection and prone to revert to wildness if allowed to escape. Anti-pattern: species that thrive on constant alertness and excitement (frequent flight or fight behaviour) are poor candidates for permanent domestication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness to Man (economic or practical utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The animal should be useful to man (food, work, barter, ornament, etc.); otherwise there is no durable motive to maintain it into maturity and invest in breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a tamed seal that becomes troublesome was not preserved because it lacked utility, despite affection; many early menageries arose from pleasure or prestige rather than utility, but long-term domestication requires perceived usefulness. Scoring: evaluate potential utility as food, labor, secondary products, or trade value; consider historical market demand as a driver of domestication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breeding Proclivity in Captivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The species must breed freely and readily in confinement; without successful breeding in human-controlled conditions, a domestic population cannot be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: guinea-fowl do not breed in confinement and so remain merely kept as pets rather than true domestic stock. Guidance: check reproductive behaviour under confinement, ease of raising young, and generation-to-generation viability as indicators of domestication potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral Compatibility / Mutual Intelligibility with Humans or Domestic Species
rubrics_metrics.description: Species whose behaviour, modes of movement, cries, and 'language of action' are mutually intelligible or agreeable with humans (or with other domestic species) are more likely to become companions of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the dog is the exemplary companion because its movements and vocalisations map readily to human emotions and commands; two animal species will intermix only if their behaviour is reciprocally agreeable. Assess communication compatibility, temperament matching, and whether the species' social signals are interpretable and manageable by humans or established domestic animals.
